Mauna Loa. An active basaltic shield volcano on the Big Island of Hawaii, Mauna Loa is the largest subaerial volcano on Earth by both mass and volume, covering over two thousand square miles, which is approximately fifty-one percent of the land area of the Big Island. As a classic basaltic shield volcano, it is characterized by extremely broad, gentle slopes that contrast with the steep profiles of stratovolcanoes. The name translates to Long Mountain in the Hawaiian language, referring to its massive, dome-like shape and long rift zones. Mauna Loa erupted most recently in late 2022, ending a thirty-eight year period of quiet and sending lava flows within miles of the Daniel K. Inouye Highway. The volcano hosts the Mauna Loa Observatory, which has continuously measured atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations since 1958, producing the famous Keeling Curve that documents global climate change. Mauna Loa's highly active neighboring shield volcano is Kilauea, located on the southeastern flank, while Mount Erebus, another active volcano, also hosts specialized scientific research stations on its slopes.
